text: The Kingston Symphony (KS) is a Canadian orchestra based in Kingston, Ontario, with Evan Mitchell serving as its principal conductor since 2014. The ensemble primarily performs its concerts at The Grand Theatre. The orchestra was established in 1953 as the New Symphony Association of Kingston, with Graham George as its first principal conductor. George led the debut concert of Joseph Haydn's The Creation on 12 April 1954 at The Grand Theatre, featuring the Kingston Choral Society and baritone James Milligan. In its first three years, the orchestra held only two concerts annually, but the number of performances increased starting in 1957. Subsequent principal conductors included William Hill (1957–1959) and Edouard Bartlett (1960–1965). In 1963, the ensemble was renamed the Kingston Symphony, coinciding with the formation of the Kingston Symphony Association. Some concerts were held at the Kingston Gospel Temple. Alexander Brott became conductor in 1965 and oversaw the hiring of several professional string and wind players. The newly renovated Grand Theatre became the orchestra's primary concert venue. Brian Jackson served as conductor from 1982 to 1991, during which time the Symphony performed approximately twelve concerts per year. In 1992, Glen Fast assumed the conductorship. Under his leadership, the orchestra shifted toward performing new works by Canadian composers, including world premieres of Chan Ka Nin's Violin Concerto (1998), Marjan Mozetich's Piano Concerto (2000), Srul Irving Glick's last work, Isaiah (2002), John Burge's Clarinet Concerto (2004), István Anhalt's The Tents of Abraham (2005), and Peter Paul Koprowski's Tapestries of Love: Symphony for Soprano and Orchestra (2007). Fast remained conductor until 2014, when Evan Mitchell succeeded him.
